newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO cooperate to keep calm in Hebron.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO cooperate to keep calm in Hebron.

text.p: Israel and Yasser Arafat's Palestinian Authority joined forces on Monday to restore calm to the volatile streets of the divided West Bank town of Hebron.
Israel warned the Palestinians that it would be forced to act with a "heavy hand" against any renewed Arab unrest in Hebron.

Near PLO-ruled Bethlehem, a Palestinian youth was seriously wounded when an Israeli soldier shot him in the head with a rubber bullet during brief clashes that erupted on Monday night in the West Bank village of Beit Sahour. Hospital sources said Ashraf Dawawra, 19, was in a stable condition.
In Hebron, some 200 Palestinian policemen stood on the invisible border dividing the 80 percent of Hebron handed over to PLO self-rule in January from the 20 percent of it still held by Israel.
The Palestinian security men pounced on a handful of youths who tried to stone Israeli troops. For its part, Israel allowed Arab shops to open.

Joint patrols resumed, in sharp contrast to the almost daily unrest of the last three weeks. Troops have shot and wounded scores of Palestinians hurling stones and fire bombs that wounded several soldiers.

"If the Palestinian Authority wants to calm the situation, to get back on the discussion track and renew the diplomatic process, it will find in us a partner," Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told reporters in Jerusalem.

"But if this violence continues, it will require us to take very firm steps, including measures that I don't want to elaborate on now," he said, accusing the Authority of organising and abetting anti-Israeli violence.

Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai's office said in a statement Israel had passed "sharp messages" to the PA. "If the security situation in Hebron continues as it was until last night, the defence establishment will be forced to act with a heavy hand in order to restore order," the statement said.
Asked whether the Palestinian police deployment in Hebron signalled a change in attitude, Netanyahu replied: "Only time will tell."

Israel's Hebron brigade commander, identified for security reasons only as Colonel Gadi, said his Palestinian counterparts had promised at a meeting on Sunday to restore calm and asked Israel to ease restrictions on Palestinians in the city.

Israel had imposed measures he said were meant to bolster Israeli security -- closing off alleys, closing Palestinian shops and erecting concrete roadblocks. Some 400 Jewish settlers live on the side still held by Israel.
"We decided this morning to begin with a small step and that's to allow (Palestinian) trade to open on two streets where trade had been closed near the Jewish Quarter," Gadi said.
Palestinian police commander Colonel Tariq Zaid said the Israelis promised to do their best to restore life to normal.

Zaid told reporters the Palestinian police had deployed in the area to keep Israel from carrying out what he said was a plan both to take back part of the self-ruled area handed over in January and to renegotiate its status.

Formal peace talks have been frozen since Israel broke ground on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem four months ago. The latest unrest was sparked by posters a Jewish woman put up in Hebron depicting Islam's Prophet Mohammad as a pig.
Israeli troops wounded 16 Arabs, including five journalists, in clashes on Sunday. The army denied it deliberately shot the journalists, all Palestinians employed by foreign news media.
A Palestinian negotiator said Israel and the PLO had agreed on take-off and landing procedures and a name for an airport in the self-ruled Gaza Strip.
Palestinian cabinet minister Nabil Shaath said progress on opening the airport, a Gaza sea port and a corridor between the strip and the West Bank could help revive formal peace talks.
